title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics

epigraph.quote: In heavy electrical and thermal equipment, gross margin is won in the factory schedule and lost in the freight and working capital cycle.
epigraph.author: Manufacturing Operations Principle

web_blocks.html: Vertiv operates a hybrid go-to-market model tailored to customer scale [1]. For hyperscalers, cloud providers, and major colocation operators, Vertiv uses a direct enterprise sales and solution-architect force [1, 14]. Those teams engage 12 to 24 months ahead of site commissioning to lock in technical specifications [1, 14]. For mid-market enterprise, telecom, and commercial-industrial accounts, Vertiv sells through value-added resellers (VARs), IT distributors, and electrical OEM partners [1].

Vertiv manufactures across global facilities in North America, EMEA, and APAC, yet its production footprint still trails its geographic revenue shift [1, 41]. Per the FY2025 Form 10-K, 58.8% ($6,013.6 million of $10,229.9 million) of net sales shipped to United States destinations, up from 51.0% in 2024 [1]. By contrast, Q3 2026 Form 10-Q Note 8 shows only 43.6% ($577.8 million of $1,324.6 million) of net property, plant, and equipment sits in the United States [41]. Because 56.4% of net fixed assets sit outside the United States, cross-border tariff policy remains an active cost friction [1, 41]. After the U.S. Supreme Court invalidated IEEPA tariffs in February 2026, U.S. Customs launched its CAPE refund portal in April and June 2026 [41]. Vertiv has not recognized any refund gain contingencies under ASC 450-30, and prior Mexico SAT customs audits ($10.1 million paid in 2024) underscore cross-border compliance risk [1, 41].

web_blocks.html: Every line of the FY2025 waterfall reconciles directly to Vertiv's audited Form 10-K. Out of $10,229.90 million in net sales, cost of sales absorbs $6,514.70 million (63.7%), leaving $3,715.20 million in gross profit (36.3%) [1]. Operating expenses ex-D&A take $1,576.90 million (15.4%), yielding $2,138.30 million in GAAP EBITDA (20.9%) and—after $308.60 million of D&A—$1,829.70 million in GAAP operating profit (17.9%) [1, 22, 23]. Subtracting $86.10 million in net interest, $1.70 million in other expense, and $409.10 million in taxes leaves $1,332.80 million in GAAP net income (13.03 per $100) [1]. Adding back non-cash D&A of $308.60 million (+3.02 per $100) plus $472.40 million (+4.62 per $100) in working-capital and non-cash bridges equals $2,113.80 million in CFO (20.66 per $100, within $0.01 rounding) [22, 46]. Deducting $226.40 million in capex (-2.21) delivers $1,887.40 million in FCF (+18.45) [22, 46].

Cash conversion stayed strong in 2026 even as capital intensity nearly doubled [41, 42]. In 9M 2026, operating cash flow hit $2,660.6 million while capital expenditures including software jumped to $430.3 million ($425.0 million PP&E plus $5.3 million software) [41]. That lifts capex intensity to 4.2% of 9M 2026 sales, versus 2.2% ($226.4 million) in FY2025, with full-year 2026 capex guided to $575 million–$600 million (~4.0% of revenue) [1, 41, 42]. Meanwhile, customer prepayments pushed current deferred revenue to $4,120.5 million ($4,245.7 million including $125.2 million noncurrent) at September 30, 2026, up from $1,814.7 million current at year-end 2025 [41].

Working-capital absorption requires fresh scrutiny after rapid 2026 inventory growth [41]. Between December 31, 2025 and September 30, 2026, inventories more than doubled (+125.8%) from $1,456.5 million to $3,288.4 million [41]. Raw materials surged 143.6% to $1,658.1 million, while finished products rose 120.5% to $1,224.7 million [41]. Accounts receivable also grew 40.9% YTD to $4,379.7 million (92.7 days on Q3 annualized sales), cushioned by $3,244.7 million in accounts payable and $4,120.5 million in current deferred revenue [41].

book_paragraphs: Understanding Vertiv's economics requires looking past the glamour of artificial intelligence chips and examining how heavy electrical and thermal hardware actually moves from a factory floor to a customer site. Vertiv runs two distinct sales channels. For the world's largest hyperscalers and colocation landlords, its own solution architects sit at the design table 12 to 24 months before a concrete slab is poured. For mid-sized enterprises, hospitals, and regional telecoms, it relies on distributors, value-added resellers, and OEM partners.

Behind those channels sits a global manufacturing network of 30 plants, expanded from 24 just a few years ago. Rather than shipping bulky chillers and switchgear across oceans—a mistake that crushed margins in 2022—Vertiv builds close to demand: Ohio and Texas for North America, Tognana in Italy for Europe, and Johor in Malaysia for Asia Pacific. Hyperscalers put these factories through grueling qualification audits, testing equipment under full thermal and electrical load before signing multi-year supply agreements.

Two 2026 updates sharpen this unit-economics picture. First, capital spending stepped up from 2.2 percent of sales in FY2025. Nine-month 2026 capex including software jumped to 430.3 million dollars, or 4.2 percent of revenue. Vertiv is expanding capacity while inventories more than doubled to 3.29 billion dollars. Second, tariff risk remains meaningful. In FY2025, 58.8 percent of revenue shipped to the United States. Yet only 43.6 percent of net plant and equipment sat inside US borders at September 30, 2026.

book_subsections.title: Follow One Hundred Dollars Through the FY2025 Income Statement
paragraphs: Let us trace 100 dollars of audited FY2025 revenue through Vertiv's financial engine. Out of 10,229.9 million dollars in total net sales, 63 dollars and 68 cents went straight to cost of sales—copper, steel, fans, power electronics, factory labor, and embedded engineering. That left 36 dollars and 32 cents in gross profit, a massive recovery from the 28 dollars and 40 cents Vertiv kept in 2022.

From that gross profit, Vertiv spent 15 dollars and 81 cents on selling, general, and administrative overhead, plus another 2 dollars and 62 cents on intangible amortization, restructuring, and minor operating items. That left 17 dollars and 89 cents in GAAP operating profit. After paying just 86 cents in net interest and 4 dollars in income taxes, Vertiv brought 13 dollars and 3 cents to the bottom line as GAAP net income.

Here is the part that separates a disciplined operator from an ordinary manufacturer: Vertiv generated 20 dollars and 66 cents in operating cash flow per 100 dollars of sales, spent only 2 dollars and 21 cents on capital expenditures, and pocketed 18 dollars and 45 cents in free cash flow. How can free cash flow exceed net income by more than 40 percent? Two reasons: Vertiv's plants are assembly and test-bay operations rather than capital-hungry foundries, and hyperscalers increasingly put down cash deposits for custom AI gear—pushing deferred revenue to 3.63 billion dollars by mid-2026.

callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
callouts.text: Customer prepayments are a wonderful source of zero-cost working capital during an expansion, but remember the mirror image: if hyperscale order intake ever decelerates sharply, deferred revenue unwinds and cash conversion normalizes back toward net income.

book_subsections.title: How Engineering Co-Design Replaces Pure Price Competition
paragraphs: In ordinary industrial equipment, a purchasing manager sends out a spreadsheet, collects three bids, and awards the contract to the lowest price. Data center power and liquid cooling work differently because a single thermal runaway or power-transfer failure inside a billion-dollar AI cluster costs tens of millions of dollars per hour in lost compute.

Vertiv sells through two distinct channels that reinforce each other. For hyperscalers and major colocation operators, Vertiv's direct engineering teams co-design reference architectures 12 to 24 months ahead of silicon launches—qualifying coolant distribution units, busways, and rack manifolds directly alongside chipmakers like NVIDIA. Once a design is written into a hyperscaler's standard build specification, switching to an untested rival mid-campus introduces unacceptable schedule and warranty risk.

For mid-market enterprises, telecom operators, and regional colocation facilities, Vertiv relies on value-added resellers, electrical distributors, and mechanical contractors. That two-tier go-to-market engine explains why Vertiv's $100 revenue waterfall converts so cleanly into cash: gross margin sits at 36.3 percent, capital expenditures consume just 2.2 percent of sales, and customer prepayments help fund factory expansion.

book_subsections.title: Tracing Every Dollar From Factory Floor to Free Cash Flow
paragraphs: Look closely at the FY2025 $100 unit-economics waterfall in the web edition and notice how lean Vertiv's physical capital intensity remains. Out of every $100 of net sales ($10,229.9 million total), cost of goods sold consumes $63.70, leaving $36.30 of gross profit. Selling, general, and administrative expenses—including roughly $442 million of engineering, research, and development—take $15.80, while intangible amortization, restructuring, and other items absorb $2.60, leaving $17.90 of GAAP operating profit.

From there, net interest takes just $0.80 thanks to rapid deleveraging, and taxes take $4.00, yielding $13.00 of GAAP net income. Now watch the cash conversion magic: adding back $3.00 of non-cash depreciation and amortization alongside net working-capital inflows lifts operating cash flow to $20.70 per $100 of sales, while capital expenditures require only $2.20. That leaves $18.50 of free cash flow on every $100 of revenue—a cash engine powerful enough to self-fund capacity expansion and bolt-on acquisitions simultaneously.

In 2026, that asset-light capex ratio moved higher. Nine-month 2026 capital spending including software reached 430.3 million dollars, or 4.2 percent of sales. Full-year capex is guided near 4.0 percent. Current deferred revenue expanded to 4.12 billion dollars by September 30, 2026. Yet inventories doubled to 3.29 billion dollars, and IEEPA tariff refund claims remain unrecognized until collected.

book_subsections.title: Customer Qualification: Why Switching Mid-Campus Rarely Happens
paragraphs: Think about the engineering timeline inside a modern AI data center. A hyperscaler does not buy a coolant distribution unit off a catalog shelf on Tuesday and plug it in on Friday. The thermal loop must be validated for flow rate, pressure drop, chemical compatibility with copper and aluminum cold plates, and automated failover months before the first server rack arrives.

Once Vertiv's equipment clears that qualification gate and gets written into the campus blueprint, a rival offering a 5 percent discount on hardware rarely wins a mid-project swap. The risk of delaying a billion-dollar GPU cluster by even thirty days dwarfs any small hardware savings, giving Vertiv genuine pricing and schedule power during active buildouts.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Spending just 2.2 percent of sales on capex while growing revenue over 27 percent in a single year is an enviable industrial profile. It tells you Vertiv's bottleneck is engineering talent and qualified floor space, not massive fixed-asset intensity.
